column5: God's Spirit and words placed in a mouth, never departing
column6: The commentary takes 87:6 as God's promise to make the recipient recite and retain the given word. Isaiah's covenant places God's Spirit and words in a recipient's mouth and promises that they will not leave that mouth or its descendants, extending secure recitation into a line of transmission.

column5: a song written, taught, and put in Israel's mouth
column6: The commentary's instructor first gives the recitation and the recipient then carries it. God tells Moses to write the song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths; the verse combines written preservation, teaching, and voiced reception.

column5: the covenant song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
column6: The promised “you will not forget” is a result of divine action in the commentary. Deuteronomy makes the song a witness precisely because it will not be forgotten from Israel's descendants' mouths, a communal analogue to retained recitation.

column5: the Spirit teaches and brings Jesus' words to remembrance
column6: The commentary insists that unforgetting is granted rather than commanded. Jesus promises that the Paraclete will teach the disciples and bring all his sayings to their remembrance, a direct Christian promise of divinely caused recall.

column5: YHWH with Moses' mouth, teaching what to speak
column6: The direct divine “we” and enabled human speech are central to the commentary. At Moses' reluctance, YHWH promises to be with his mouth and teach him what to say, making speech possible without making Moses its independent source.

column5: YHWH puts words into a prophet's mouth
column6: The commentary pictures the word moving from its source into the recipient's tongue. In Jeremiah's call, YHWH touches the prophet's mouth and says that the divine words have been put there, a particularly close prophetic counterpart.

column5: taught tongue and repeatedly awakened ear
column6: The commentary's causative reading has the recipient hear the teacher before speaking for others. Isaiah's servant receives a taught tongue and an ear awakened morning by morning to hear as a learner, joining receptive hearing to fitting speech.

column5: the Holy Spirit teaches what must be said
column6: The commentary treats 87:6 as a future assurance that God enables the addressee's utterance. Jesus tells disciples that the Holy Spirit will teach them, at the needed moment, what they ought to say; the setting is different, but the divine provision of speech is equally explicit.

column5: word in mouth and heart for enactment
column6: The commentary describes the given word as held within the recipient and then given outwardly. Deuteronomy says the command is very near, in mouth and heart, in order to do it; it joins inner retention, oral expression, and lived obedience.

column5: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
column6: The commentary's B001/B002 labels develop ق ر ء as recitation that carries joined words to hearers. Moses reads the covenant book aloud to Israel in this verse; Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ) is the clear cognate and its covenant setting shows reading as received, binding speech.

column5: a scroll eaten before the prophet speaks
column6: The commentary's womb-and-heart image has revelation taken inside before it is released as public speech. Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll and then go speak to Israel, making ingestion the concrete bridge between receiving written words and proclaiming them.

column5: words received from God spoken to Israel
column6: After the scroll scene, Ezekiel is sent to Israel with God's own words. This supplies the outward half of the commentary's sequence: a word retained in the prophet becomes warning addressed to others.

column5: the little scroll eaten, sweet in mouth and bitter within
column6: The commentary compares a word held in the body to a pregnancy before its outward delivery. Revelation recasts Ezekiel's act: John takes and eats a scroll, experiencing it in mouth and stomach, an embodied reception of prophecy rather than mere reading.

column5: prophecy required after eating the scroll
column6: The commentary moves from retained recitation to the task of reminding others. After the scroll is eaten, John is told that he must prophesy again about peoples and kings; this supplies the public-release side of the same received-word image.

column5: Torah placed within and written on hearts
column6: The commentary says that the word is gathered and held in the recipient rather than merely external to him. Jeremiah's new-covenant promise has God put Torah within the people and write it on their hearts, a scriptural inner-inscription analogue.

column5: the word dwelling richly, teaching, admonishing, and singing
column6: The commentary links unforgotten recitation to later reminder, worship, and a life shaped by the word. Colossians asks that Christ's word dwell richly in the community so that it teaches and admonishes through sung praise, joining inward residence to communal utterance.

column5: the good deposit guarded through the indwelling Spirit
column6: The commentary calls the received word an entrusted deposit whose retention depends on the giver. Timothy is told to guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit dwelling in believers, a Christian account of preserved teaching with divine, not merely human, custody.

column5: Arabic ن س ي B001/B002/B003 and Hebrew נשה (nāšâ)
column6: The commentary's ن س ي material makes forgetting both failure to retain an entrusted word and, through the womb image, a falling-away from what was held. Deuteronomy says Israel is unmindful of the Rock that begot it and forgets the God who gave it birth; Hebrew נשה (nāšâ) is cognate with Arabic ن س ي, and the verse uniquely joins forgetting to birthing.

column5: a nursing mother who might forget, but God does not
column6: The commentary contrasts human forgetfulness with the God who does not forget, while using maternal containment as a secondary image. Isaiah invokes a nursing mother and her child only to insist that even if she forgets, God will not forget Zion, binding maternal care and unfailing divine memory.

column5: do not forget what was received; make it known to children
column6: The commentary's recipient is preserved from forgetting so that he can later remind others. Deuteronomy warns Israel not to forget what it has witnessed and immediately turns that memory into teaching children and grandchildren, giving a covenantal counterpart to retention becoming reminder.

column5: withered grass and the word that stands forever
column6: The commentary places the promise that the recited word will not fall away beside pasture turned into dark refuse. Isaiah's one verse contrasts grass and flower fading with God's word standing forever, making the vegetation-to-enduring-word relationship unusually close.

column5: the enduring word identified as announced good news
column6: The commentary joins an unfailing word to its passage from the recipient to other hearers. Peter says the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it as the good news announced to the audience, coupling permanence with oral proclamation.

column5: a burned scroll recreated and expanded by dictation
column6: The commentary grounds preservation in the divine source rather than the recipient's unaided memory. After Jehoiakim burns the first scroll, Jeremiah dictates its former words to another scroll and additional words are added; the scene tests the durability of revealed wording against material loss.

column5: God's word goes from the divine mouth and accomplishes its purpose
column6: The commentary presents the recited speech as originating with God and reaching its assigned result. Isaiah's word goes out from God's mouth, does not return empty, and accomplishes the sender's purpose, a source-to-effect account of effective revelation.

column5: the book kept in the mouth, meditated on, and enacted
column6: The commentary rejects a reading that remains only on the tongue and ends with recitation joined to worshipful practice. Joshua is told that the book of Torah must not depart from his mouth, but be meditated on day and night so that he does what is written; it makes durable recitation a form of life.

column5: prophets speaking from God while carried by the Spirit
column6: The commentary distinguishes the human reader from the God who supplies the word. Second Peter says prophetic speech did not arise by human will but that people spoke from God while borne by the Holy Spirit, expressing a comparable account of sourced prophetic utterance.

column5: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
column6: The commentary treats recitation as joined words whose meaning is also opened for hearers. Nehemiah's assembly reads from the Torah and gives its sense so the people understand the reading; Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ), cognate with the commentary's ق ر ء, appears in a communal reading-and-explanation setting.

column5: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
column6: The commentary's recitation is held so that it governs the recipient's way of life. The king must keep a Torah scroll with him and read it all his days in order to learn reverence and keep its words; the Hebrew cognate קרא makes daily reading an antidote to abandonment.

column5: God's word stored in the heart
column6: The commentary says the word is gathered within so it will not be lost. The psalmist stores God's saying in the heart in order not to sin, a devotional response that makes inner retention ethically consequential.

column5: one reader, hearers, and keepers of prophecy
column6: The commentary traces a word from its divine source through a reader to those reminded by it. Revelation blesses the one who reads its prophecy aloud and those who hear and keep it, a liturgical community shaped by public recitation and retention.

column5: Christ's letter written by the Spirit on human hearts
column6: The commentary's pages are not opposed to interior retention: words are gathered in the recipient before they are uttered. Paul calls the Corinthian community Christ's letter, written by the living God's Spirit on hearts rather than stone, a Christian transformation of scroll imagery into inward inscription.

column5: Deuteronomy's mouth-and-heart word read as proclaimed faith
column6: The commentary brings a word into the mouth and heart before it goes out to others. Paul quotes the mouth-and-heart formulation of Deuteronomy and explicitly identifies it as the word of faith that he proclaims, a Christian interpretive reuse of the Torah's language of near, speakable instruction.

column5: heard teaching entrusted for further teaching
column6: The commentary's protected path carries a received message onward instead of leaving it with one recipient. Timothy is to entrust what he heard before witnesses to reliable people who can teach others, giving a four-stage chain of retained and retransmitted instruction.

column5: tradition held in oral word and letter
column6: The commentary repeatedly holds oral recitation beside pages and written preservation. Paul tells the Thessalonians to stand firm and hold the traditions taught either by spoken word or letter, a compact Christian pairing of memorized and written transmission.

column5: the doer rather than the forgetful hearer
column6: The commentary defines forgetting as leaving an entrusted word and contrasts a merely vocal reading with a life of worship and understanding. James contrasts a forgetful hearer with one who continues in the perfect law and acts on it, making retention visible in conduct.

column5: God remembers sin no more as covenantal action
column6: The commentary stresses that forgetting can mean abandoning rather than a simple failure of mental recall. Jeremiah's promise that God will no longer remember sin uses memory as a covenantal act of judgment or forgiveness, helping a reader hear the commentary's stronger relational sense of forgetting.

column5: forgetting even one word of Torah study
column6: The commentary says 87:6 is assurance rather than a command imposed on the recipient. Avot treats forgetting a word of one's study as grave while qualifying unavoidable loss, placing rabbinic discipline of Torah memory beside the Qur'anic promise that the messenger will not forget.

column5: “write this song” read as preserving Torah in writing
column6: The commentary ends by bringing retained recitation beside earlier pages associated with Moses. Sifre reads Deuteronomy's command to write the song as an injunction to write the Torah, a rabbinic expansion of oral teaching into durable manuscript practice.

column5: the enduring book of commandments held fast
column6: The commentary contrasts gathered, retained revelation with a word discarded as debris. Baruch calls Torah the book of God's commandments that endures forever and sets holding it fast over against death, a Jewish formulation of preservation as life-giving fidelity.

column5: the Law burned and people left without its light
column6: The commentary considers both God's power over revealed speech and the danger of a word being lost. Ezra's lament that the Law has been burned makes the loss of written revelation a concrete crisis rather than merely a lapse of personal memory.

column5: Ezra asks for the Spirit so he can write what was lost
column6: The commentary makes the giver responsible for collecting and securing revelation. In response to the loss of the Law, Ezra asks for the Holy Spirit so that he can write what is needed for later people; the scene is a Jewish restoration analogue to divinely sustained transmission.

column5: instruction neither too difficult nor too distant
column6: The augment links the promise to recite with God's making the way easy. Deuteronomy says the command is not too difficult or beyond reach, a Torah-side claim that accessible instruction can actually be received and enacted.

column5: an easy yoke and light burden
column6: The commentary places the promised unforgotten word beside the later assurance of ease, while also noting a “weighty word.” Jesus' easy yoke and light burden provide a Christian image for divine teaching that does not finally crush the recipient.

column5: mortal life compared to grass and a fading flower
column6: The commentary has the pasture become dark chaff immediately before the promise of retained recitation. Peter's verse compares all flesh and glory to grass and a flower that withers, supplying the perishable side of the contrast developed explicitly in the next verse.

column5: the passing cosmos and imperishable words
column6: The commentary sets a word that will not be dropped against perishing vegetation. Jesus contrasts heaven and earth passing away with his words not passing away, a Christian saying of verbal permanence that sharpens the commentary's preservation claim.

column5: Mary's conception and birth announced by divine speech
column6: The commentary's secondary image follows Mary as she carries a child and withdraws to give birth. Luke's annunciation likewise joins divine speech to Mary's conception and bearing of a son; the shared Marian scene gives a canonical Christian setting for the commentary's pregnancy image.

column5: Mary keeps and ponders words in her heart
column6: The commentary lets Mary's bodily carrying illuminate a word held within rather than lost. Luke depicts Mary retaining and pondering the reported words in her heart, a Christian maternal image of memory that complements the commentary's contrast between carrying and being forgotten.

column5: Adam's transgression narrated as seeing, taking, eating, and giving
column6: The commentary invokes the Qur'anic Adam who “forgot” an entrusted command as the negative foil to 87:6. Genesis narrates the corresponding fall through the woman's seeing, taking, eating, and giving the fruit, rather than naming Adam's act forgetfulness; the difference changes how disobedience is framed.

column5: Abraham obeys commands, statutes, and laws without pages
column6: The commentary's final page-image attributes earlier sheets to Abraham and Moses. Genesis retrospectively credits Abraham with obeying divine commands and laws but mentions no Abrahamic scroll; that absence is a cautious textual contrast to the Qur'anic “pages of Abraham.”
